knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=(1-{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy-4}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy-4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{x\cdot {x}^{2}-4}}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{x\cdot {x}^{2}-4}}=\frac{x}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}+\frac{x}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=- x^{2} + x y$ and $y=- \sin{\left(4 x \right)},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=- 2 x + y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =- 2 x - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 4 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}+\left(x\right)\cdot \left(- 4 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\right) \\  & =- 4 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=- x^{2} - 2 x y$ and $y=- \sin{\left(2 x \right)},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=- 2 x - 2 y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=- 2 x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =- 2 x + 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =- 2 x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x + 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}+\left(- 2 x\right)\cdot \left(- 2 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) \\  & =4 x \cos{\left(2 x \right)} - 2 x + 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} \\  & =2 \left(2 x \cos{\left(2 x \right)} - x + \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right).\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=2 x e^{- 3 y}$ and $y=\sin{\left(4 x \right)},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=2 e^{- 3 y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=- 6 x e^{- 3 y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2 e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =- 6 x e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2 e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}+\left(- 6 x e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}\right)\cdot \left(4 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\right) \\  & =- 24 x e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}} \cos{\left(4 x \right)} + 2 e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}} \\  & =- 2 \left(12 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - 1\right) e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: - 24 x e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}} \cos{\left(4 x \right)} + 2 e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}
- 6 x e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}} \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + 2 e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}
24 x e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}} \cos{\left(4 x \right)} + 2 e^{- 3 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=- x^{2} + x y$ and $y=- x \sin{\left(4 x \right)},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=- 2 x + y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =- x \sin{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1x) & =-1, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sin{\left(4 x \right)}) & =4 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-1\cdot \left(\sin{\left(4 x \right)}\right)+\left(-1x\right)\cdot \left(4 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\right) \\  & =- 4 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =- x \sin{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x+\left(x\right)\cdot \left(- 4 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\right) \\  & =- 4 x^{2} \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x \sin{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x \\  & =- 2 x \left(2 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} + \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + 1\right).\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: - x \left(- 4 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\right) - x \sin{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x
x \left(- 4 x \cos{\left(4 x \right)} - \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\right) - x \sin{\left(4 x \right)} - 2 x
